title: Navigating a Brave New World

author: David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source does not address AI-driven operating-model transformation or bargaining shifts toward legal departments, ALSPs and AI-native providers. Instead, it frames legal-market adaptation through law firms’ expansion into nonlegal advisory services, while highlighting regulatory and cultural limits on integration and the importance of responding to client demand.
qs: Through all these initiatives, however, critical questions remain, including the extent to which law firms will be able to deeply integrate nonlegal products into their traditional business cores, whether due to regulations or internal cultural norms.

Nevertheless, it is clear that change has come to the legal services market, and the successes or failures of law firms going forward may well be defined by how well they grow and adapt—and by how well they can respond to client needs and demands.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source offers adjacent operating-model lessons about integrating lawyers and nonlawyer consultants, including cultural integration and service diversification. However, it does not address legal AI’s jagged task-level capabilities, verification requirements or selective deployment, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: If the purpose was to offer extended services to clients, it was critical to get lawyers and consultants working together.

To diversify their services and increase top-line revenues, as well as to respond to clients demanding more-integrated problem solving, innovative firms like Eversheds are leading the way toward combining deep legal expertise with nonlegal offerings.

st.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
st.an: The source accepts that competition is converging on integrated business services rather than straightforward Big Four replacement of law firms. It materially extends that proposition through Eversheds’ concrete law-firm response: incorporating adjacent consulting capabilities, recruiting multidisciplinary talent, and using senior-lawyer support and physical proximity to make integration operational, while leaving ultimate competitive outcomes unresolved.
qs: What this move does seem to reflect is that both sides recognize that insofar as clients are seeking integrated solutions, there is an urgent need to incorporate and integrate more adjacent services and functions to their core businesses.

Richardson explains that getting buy-in from senior lawyers and transitioning with them to consulting was critical in forming the link between the lawyers and the consultants and bridging any potential cultural or trust gaps.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s business-model and competitive-convergence themes with concrete examples of law firms expanding into adjacent advisory services. It adds that successful diversification depends on integrating nonlegal offerings and responding to client demand, while leaving regulatory and cultural barriers unresolved. It does not directly address AI, pricing or staffing leverage.

Nevertheless, it is clear that change has come to the legal services market, and the successes or failures of law firms going forward may well be defined by how well they grow and adapt—and by how well they can respond to client needs and demands.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that client pressure and multidisciplinary delivery are reshaping law-firm boundaries. It materially extends that proposition by showing that firms were creating consulting and corporate-advisory offerings before generative AI, while identifying regulation and internal culture as constraints on integrating nonlegal services into the traditional firm.
qs: Increasingly sophisticated clients are demanding much more from their law firms for much less, including problem solving that straddles across disciplinary lines, such as law and business, technology, and strategy (see “[A Global Age of More for Less](https://thepractice.law.harvard.edu/issue/volume-1-issue-1/)”).

Through all these initiatives, however, critical questions remain, including the extent to which law firms will be able to deeply integrate nonlegal products into their traditional business cores, whether due to regulations or internal cultural norms.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts that client pressure and output-based measurement are reshaping legal delivery, then materially extends the cluster’s adaptation thesis with a concrete incumbent-law-firm model: integrating nonlawyer consultants and experienced lawyers to provide multidisciplinary solutions. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that regulation and firm culture may constrain deeper operational integration, though it does not directly address AI-driven workflow unbundling, junior training or verification.
qs: Moreover, the increasing reliance on quality metrics and other output-based performance measures are upending traditional ways of measuring work.

Unlike the Big Four, however, by bringing subject-matter expert consultants directly into a law firm context and teaming them up with the firm’s experienced lawyers, Richardson explains that the firm can “deliver new solutions within a big law environment.”  >  Eversheds Consulting delivers new solutions within a big law environment.

st.t: Provider convergence: Buyers coordinate an unbundled market
st.an: The source supports convergence around client-focused, multidisciplinary solutions and the need for incumbent law firms to adapt. Its Eversheds framing also aligns with incumbent resilience through innovation within a traditional firm structure, but the excerpt does not establish specific integration initiatives, buyer-led unbundling or outcomes.
qs: Increasingly sophisticated clients are demanding much more from their law firms for much less, including problem solving that straddles across disciplinary lines, such as law and business, technology, and strategy (see “[A Global Age of More for Less](https://thepractice.law.harvard.edu/issue/volume-1-issue-1/)”).

Below we review some of the innovations that are occurring in light of the shifting legal marketplace by highlighting initiatives being undertaken by the U.K.-based law firm Eversheds—a firm that the *Financial Times*’ 2015 Innovation Report ranks as one of the top 10 game changers of the past decade.

kp.k: Integrated services reshape competition before contemporary legal AI
kp.d: This January/February 2016 article examines legal-market restructuring through Eversheds rather than AI. It reports Wilkins and Esteban's argument that accounting firms are expanding into legal services, especially in Europe and emerging economies, to supply integrated business solutions. The article identifies demanding clients, regulatory openings, output-based performance measures and globalization as concurrent pressures on traditional firms.
qs: the accounting firms are aggressively moving into legal services as part of their wider efforts to offer clients so-called integrated business solutions, particularly in Europe and the emerging economies.

Increasingly sophisticated clients are demanding much more from their law firms for much less, including problem solving that straddles across disciplinary lines, such as law and business, technology, and strategy
Moreover, the increasing reliance on quality metrics and other output-based performance measures are upending traditional ways of measuring work.

kp.k: Consulting diversification responds to revenue and client pressures
kp.d: Graham Richardson attributes Eversheds Consulting's origins to post-2008 financial-crisis pressures: difficulty growing revenue and too many lawyers competing for insufficient work. Officially launched in 2010 within a traditional firm, the consulting arm sought to broaden services, differentiate Eversheds and enable growth. These are stated strategic motives, not measured financial outcomes.
qs: Post-2008, the profession was going through a lot of turmoil. Growing top-line revenue was hard as there were too many lawyers chasing not enough work.
We thought this would help us deliver clients what they really needed. It would also help us grow revenue, differentiate ourselves, and hopefully equip us to grow.
Eversheds is big law—a traditional big law firm. But at the same time, we’re trying to show that we can deliver new law solutions, because we found that is what our clients want.

kp.k: Multidisciplinary services address general counsel's operational skill gaps
kp.d: Eversheds Consulting offers services in strategy, process and technology; corporate risk and compliance; human resources; and financial services regulatory compliance. Richardson argues that general counsel face operational questions, particularly technology deployment, for which legal training does not prepare them. The model combines legal expertise with management, process and technology specialists; the article names Tyco, DuPont, Lloyds Banking Group, Qatar Foundation and Walt Disney as clients but supplies no quantified performance evaluation.
qs: Consulting services are offered across four main sectors: strategy, process, and technology; corporate risk and compliance; human resources; and financial services regulatory compliance.
If you ask general counsel what problems keep them awake at night that they didn’t get trained for at law school, many will say technology.

We help them with things they were not trained for because we bring in people who have different skills than lawyers—management consultants, process people, technology people—but with the common thread that they all work in the legal space.

kp.k: Nonlawyer specialists join teams without partnership equity
kp.d: The article describes lawyers working with recruited technology and management consultants to meet needs spanning disciplinary boundaries. Nonlawyer consultants are internally treated at traditional partners' level but lack partner titles and equity; the article suggests regulatory restrictions as the likely explanation rather than establishing causation. As of publication, neither Eversheds nor any Magic Circle firm had applied for ABS status, leaving future use of regulatory openings uncertain.
qs: Second, the firm actively recruits and employs nonlawyer professionals to sit alongside and work with lawyers.

It should be made clear that while nonlawyer consultants at Eversheds are internally considered on the same level as traditional law partners, they do not carry the partner title or have equity in the firm (likely due to regulatory restrictions).
As of this writing, neither Eversheds nor any of the United Kingdom’s Magic Circle firms have thus far applied for ABS.

kp.k: Law firms compete with Big Four for talent
kp.d: Eversheds Consulting hired a former Ernst & Young partner and a former KPMG partner to lead its financial services regulatory compliance team. In the announcement quoted by the article, Paul Worth claims the practice had already won work otherwise destined for Big Four accountants or risk consultants. He presents colocated lawyers and consultants, integrated regulatory advice and legal professional privilege where appropriate as differentiators. These competitive and privilege claims are attributed to the firm, while the article explicitly leaves client preference unresolved.
qs: Eversheds Consulting recently hired away a former Ernst & Young partner and a former KPMG partner to head up its new financial services regulatory compliance team
The growth of the financial services regulatory consulting practice has already seen the firm winning work which otherwise would have gone to the “Big Four” accountants or risk consultants.
Where appropriate, it will also enable the client to rely on legal professional privilege, which is something the accountants and risk consultants cannot provide.
It is an open question as to whether clients will prefer the integrated solutions offered by the Big Four or those increasingly being offered by innovative firms such as Eversheds.

kp.k: Agile supplies flexible lawyers to in-house teams
kp.d: Established in 2011, Eversheds Agile supplies interim legal consultants flexibly to in-house teams, drawing lawyers from Eversheds alumni. In June 2015 the firm announced expansion to Hong Kong and Singapore with an initial pool of 20 to 30 lawyers. The article presents this as a specialized service developed through the consulting arm, not as a separate technology vendor.
qs: Begun in 2011, Eversheds Agile provides interim legal consultants to in-house legal teams on a flexible basis, building its base of lawyers from Eversheds alum.
Recognizing the importance of the emerging economies, in June 2015 the firm announced Agile would be rolled out in Hong Kong and Singapore with an initial pool of 20 to 30 lawyers.

kp.k: Ignite manages outsourced high-volume, low-risk legal work
kp.d: Launched in 2015, Eversheds Ignite is described by the firm as a managed outsourcing offering led by lawyers and consultants for in-house teams' high-volume, low-risk work, including nondisclosure agreements, renewals, extensions and lower-value supplier contracts. The article reports a deal signed late in the preceding year to transfer Communisis's in-house legal team to Ignite, providing a concrete example of changing legal-delivery boundaries.
qs: in 2015 the firm launched Eversheds Ignite.
According to the firm, Ignite is geared toward providing in-house legal teams a means to outsource high-volume, low-risk work
Late last year, the firm signed a deal with Communisis, a communication company, to transfer its in-house legal team to Ignite.

kp.k: Senior lawyer sponsorship helps bridge professional cultural divisions
kp.d: Richardson identifies cultural clashes as a challenge when introducing consulting into a traditional firm. To obtain mainstream lawyers' support, he recruited a senior banking lawyer and litigator into consulting. His account of an established partner trusting the new team through a longstanding relationship with the litigator illustrates the proposed mechanism: respected internal intermediaries reduce trust gaps between lawyers and consultants. This is interview-based organizational evidence rather than a systematic assessment.
qs: One of the major challenges in delivering new law offerings within a traditional law firm structure,
is making sure that there aren’t too many clashes.
To do this, Richardson recruited a banking lawyer and a litigator from the firm—both of whom were senior players and at the top of their games—to the consulting practice.
This provided the wider consulting team the context and trust necessary to do the work

kp.k: Physical integration promotes collaboration and shared opportunities
kp.d: The article argues that isolating consultants would undermine the objective of offering extended client services. Richardson describes deliberately seating consultants near relevant lawyers to foster working relationships and opportunity-sharing, presenting proximity as a practical integration mechanism rather than merely adding a separate service unit.
qs: If the purpose was to offer extended services to clients, it was critical to get lawyers and consultants working together.
We made a physical effort to integrate consultants by placing them near relevant lawyers.
If you’ve got a compliance consultant, you put them next to a financial services regulatory lawyer, and lo and behold, they do work with each other and share opportunities.

kp.k: Wider diversification remains constrained by regulation and culture
kp.d: The article situates Eversheds alongside Mayer Brown's 2014 Asian consulting launch and DLA Piper's 2015 announcement of Noble Street, a corporate advisory arm targeting media, entertainment, technology and sports. It predicts further firms will follow, while qualifying that deep integration of nonlegal offerings remains uncertain because of regulation and internal cultural norms. Its concluding view that adaptation to client needs may shape firms' success is a prospective argument, not an established outcome.
qs: For instance, in 2014, Mayer Brown launched a consulting arm in Asia, hiring an international trade advisory team.
Other firms will most likely follow in their footsteps.

Through all these initiatives, however, critical questions remain, including the extent to which law firms will be able to deeply integrate nonlegal products into their traditional business cores, whether due to regulations or internal cultural norms.
the successes or failures of law firms going forward may well be defined by how well they grow and adapt—and by how well they can respond to client needs and demands.

Its references to technology concern general technology expertise and support for in-house legal departments, not AI. This is a legal-services source without substantive AI discussion, rather than a cross-domain source.
